doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: Los Angeles and the West Coast
title: The West Coast sound and the East-West rivalry
summary: He says his heroes were East Coast players but admired Hawes, Perkins and Freeman; the rivalry was a 1950s press story, and the New York attitude never bothered him.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Did the players, like Shorty Rogers and yourself, did you consider that you were playing the west coast sound, or was that something that the east coast people put on your music?

I never thought about it because really most of my heroes were players on the east coast, but having said that I mean there were such great players out here I almost hesitate to say — when I say “most” I mean maybe more back there than in L.A. But Hampton Hawes was active and really playing at his peak, and Carl Perkins, another great pianist who also died very young, Russ Freeman, I mean there were wonderful, wonderful players out here. And again as I alluded to earlier, had they gone back east and stayed back there they would have reached a much higher level of recognition than they ever did. But for whatever reasons they chose to stay out here. But they were the first people I heard live just because of the proximity. I mean I didn’t go to the east coast until the early 1970s. So there was a long period where the only people I worked with or saw live really were primarily people out here. I saw traveling bands of course that would come out from New © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

York. I remember seeing Miles out in L.A. the first time. But you know that whole east coast/west coast thing, by the ‘60s I think it had somewhat subsided. That was more of a journalistic big deal in the ‘50s. And I think it sold a lot of records in both directions and it created kind of a stir, you know there’s nothing like some kind of a real or fictional rivalry to kind of whip things up and get a little more press maybe. But it was very real. I remember the articles that would come out about east coast and west coast, and some albums would make some reference in their titles “East Meets West,” and so it was definitely happening. But I think by the ‘60s that had kind of worn itself out. There is no question that there are people — there’s a New York attitude that — just as in the famous map, is it Steinberg? The artist? The New Yorker artist that, in a nutshell, there’s nothing west of the Hudson.
Oh he did the thing with all New York and in back there’s this teeny little—

That’s a very astute summing up of the New York attitude, I think about most everything in general, not just jazz music. And when you leave New York you’re not going anywhere is kind of the attitude. So I think to that extent I mean certainly never out here, there was never any discrimination against the east, I mean everybody out here genuinely admired everybody back there. And as I said earlier, a lot of people back there had been out here originally anyway. But there’s a lot of it. I mean to this day in New York you get a certain amount of that. That just kind of goes with the territory. And it never bothered me. I mean I admired what was going on there so much and the players so much, I felt they were entitled to that, they had earned it. If you’ve paid your dues there over a period of time, you can have whatever attitude you want as far as that’s concerned. Because it’s tough there. It’s tough to survive, the weather’s tough, so yeah, I admire those guys.
